Argument for “He Was Less Cautious Than Others”

1. Quade’s Pattern of Reckless Violations
  a. Repeated Overextension of Safety Cable  
     • “<invalid_quote>He didn’t hook on a cable… intended to go beyond the three-mile limit</invalid_quote>” despite Captain Gavin’s explicit orders to “<quote>to get any further from the ship."</quote>” (p. 34).  
     • Hazard pay motive would incline him to preserve his life and pay; instead he abandons safety repeatedly.
  b. Solo Exploration and Specimen Capture  
     • “<quote>took a suit and  a cartographer unit. He's out there somewhere, alone</quote>” (p. 31). Solo means no pay credit if lost; purely rash self-assertion.  
     • Runs ahead of four-man party to seize alien “specimen,” triggering crew’s near–fatal trampling (p. 56).
  c. Ignoring Physical Trauma  
     • After he “<quote>got frostbite and heat prostration</quote>” (p. 42), he immediately volunteers for further survey: “<quote>In  the future, I'll be able to resist sensations </quote>” (p. 63). Rather than healing and reassessing, he persists on the same dangerous tactics.

2. Quade’s “Confession” Is the Lesson of Recklessness, Not Pay
  a. “<invalid_quote>I’ve been… a blind, arrogant, cocksure fool… I’m never going to be that foolhardy again</invalid_quote>” (p. 68).  
     • A genuine change of heart about caution confirms that his prior behavior was misguided bravery, not rational profit-seeking.  
     • If he had merely calculated pay, he would not regret or alter tactics once pay prospect remained constant.
  b. Final Demotion Undermines Pay Motive  
     • Despite lamenting loss of hazard pay—“<invalid_quote>I’ll lose hazard pay… be further from retirement!</invalid_quote>” (p. 69)—he consents to reassemble and re-survey: “<invalid_quote>But they [aliens] knew our own people could help us… They want Earthmen to colonize…</invalid_quote>” (p. 68). His consent arises from duty and realizing former tactics endanger crew, not to regain pay.

3. Logical Inconsistencies in “Hazard Pay” Theory
  a. Pay Is Only Cited in Self-Defense  
     • Every mention of “hazard pay” occurs when Quade is contradicted: first to justify his retention of Ordinary rank (“<quote>I'm closer to  retirement</quote>” p. 16) and then to protest demotion. He never invokes pay when ordering new expeditions.  
     • True pay motivation would lead consistent caution when out of pay range; but Quade’s recklessness ignores pay‐preserving measures.
  b. No Net Gain When Lost  
     • His solo venture almost kills him and forces the Captain to cannibalize the ship for rescue. Any pay gained is nullified by potential mission failure and court-martial if he died.

4. The Thematic Role of Quade’s Recklessness
  a. Counterpoint to Captain’s Caution  
     • The narrative contrasts “outsider” caution (Gavin) with “experienced” spaceman boldness. Quade personifies the dangers of overconfidence: “<invalid_quote>Even I know… you can’t trust anything…</invalid_quote>” (p. 14) yet he trusts his instincts blindly.
  b. Climactic Demonstration of Risk  
     • Only when the alien “helps” that he is rescued—an external intervention, not self-interest—does survival occur. This underlines that his own methods were insufficient.

Refutation of Opponent’s Points
1. Recklessness Doesn’t Equal Rational Investment  
   • Opponent claims exploration equates to future pay. But exploration without guarantee of return pay (beyond 3-mile cable) is malpractice, not investment.
2. Solitary Expeditions Are Disallowed  
   • If pay were his motive, Quade would heed standard procedure endorsed by Nagurski, Farley and the Captain, since disciplined crew surgeries ensure mission survival (and thus future pay). His refusal shows indifference to pay in face of temptation for individual notoriety.
3. “Experienced Resistance” Is Retrospective Hubris  
   • Quade’s belief in “gauge” readings over senses (“<quote>if my gauges tell me it's a lie</quote>” p. 64) is courageous, not pay-driven. He learns that ‘experience’ must be built via safer indoctrination, not solo gambles.

Conclusion
Direct textual evidence shows Quade’s persistent, unprovoked violations of safety, disregard for self-preservation, and the ultimate need for external rescue. His isolated claims of pay are defensive rationalizations, not primary motives. The consistent theme is Quade’s excessive boldness overcoming him until he learns caution—a lesson diametrically opposed to a simple “hazard pay” calculus. “He was less cautious than others” best explains Quade’s feelings and actions.

2. Solitary Expeditions Are Disallowed

His isolated claims of pay are defensive rationalizations, not primary motives. The consistent theme is Quade’s excessive boldness overcoming him until he learns caution—a lesson diametrically opposed to a simple “hazard pay” calculus. “He was less cautious than others” best explains Quade’s feelings and actions.
